lead: A car's electrical system is a small power grid on wheels: the alternator generates, the battery stores, and dozens of loads draw from one 12 V bus through copper wires. Each wire must be thick enough to keep its voltage drop and temperature within limits, and no thicker, because a harness is heavy and costly. Circuit diagrams are the map a technician uses to follow every path from the battery to a load and back.
prereq: You need: Ohm's law (V = I × R) and power (P = V × I) from first-year physics, and the history of the 12 V system in Chapter 1.1.

sections.h3: Generator, store and loads: the vehicle power supply

blocks.text: Every conventional vehicle electrical system has three parts. The alternator generates electrical energy while the engine runs. The battery stores energy for starting and for times when the alternator cannot keep up. The loads (also called consumers) use the energy. All of them hang on one bus: a positive network fed from the battery and alternator, and a return through the steel body and engine block, called chassis ground or terminal 31.
Loads are grouped by how long they draw current, because that decides how much charge they take from the battery:

items: Permanent loads work even when parked: clock, alarm, ECU standby current. Each draws milliamperes, but over weeks they can flatten a battery.
Continuous loads run with the engine: ignition, injection, fuel pump, engine ECU.
Long-time loads run for minutes or hours: headlamps, blower, rear-window heater, wipers, radio.
Short-time loads work for seconds: starter, horn, power windows, brake lamps.

blocks.text: The charge balance compares the charge the alternator puts into the battery with the charge the loads take out. In slow night traffic the alternator at idle may give less current than the loads need, so the battery makes up the difference; on an open road the alternator covers the loads and recharges it. A design must keep the balance positive over a typical trip, or the battery goes flat after a week of short drives.

Most cars use one 12 V battery. Vehicles with large accessory loads (ambulances, caravans, buses) may use a two-battery system: a starter battery kept for cranking and a supply battery for the other loads, joined through a relay or isolator so the loads can never drain the starter battery. Heavy trucks use 24 V, two 12 V batteries in series, which halves the current for the same power. Loads on the bus are in parallel, so their currents add.

A wire is chosen by three tests: the voltage drop at full load must stay within a permitted value; the wire's temperature must stay within the limit of its insulation, which depends on the current and the bundle it sits in; and it must be mechanically strong enough for vibration and handling, so very thin wires are avoided even for tiny currents. For long feeds, such as those to the rear lamps, the voltage drop usually decides.
The resistance of a wire is R = ρl ÷ A. Putting it into the voltage drop ΔU = I × R and solving for the cross-section gives the sizing formula:

blocks.where: A is the conductor cross-section in mm²; I is the load current in A; ρ is the resistivity of copper, about 0.0172 Ω·mm²/m at 20 °C (it rises about 0.4 % per kelvin, so a hot wire drops more); l is the wire length in m; ΔU is the permitted voltage drop in V.

blocks.text: Here l is the length that carries the current. With a chassis return only the feed counts, because the steel body has almost no resistance; with a separate return wire, as sensors use, l is twice the route length. Round the result up to the next standard size: 0.35, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0, 1.5, 2.5, 4, 6, 10, 16, 25, 35 or 50 mm². Starter cables are 16 to 50 mm²; most lamp and motor feeds 0.75 to 2.5 mm².

A circuit diagram (schematic) shows how each circuit works: current paths run as straight vertical lines from the positive supply at the top to ground (terminal 31) at the bottom, and parts are drawn where the circuit is easiest to follow, not where they sit in the car. A wiring diagram shows the real positions of the parts and the harness routes, with wire colours and sizes. A terminal diagram lists every connector pin, and a location diagram shows where each part is fitted.

Standard symbols are drawn for the battery, fuse, switch, relay coil and contact, lamp, motor, diode, resistor, connector and ground. Wires carry a code such as 1.5 RD/WH: 1.5 mm², red with a white stripe. Terminals carry the DIN 72552 numbers that are stamped on the parts themselves:

head: Terminal
Meaning
rows: Positive switched by the ignition switch
Relay contact: input, normally open output (normally closed output)
Alternator output, excitation, field, charge warning lamp

blocks.text: To trace a fault, follow the line from terminal 30 or 15 through each fuse, switch and relay contact to the load, then the return to ground; every part on that path can hide a voltage drop or an open circuit.

examples.question: Two 55 W low-beam headlamps are fed through one copper wire 4.0 m long from the relay to the lamps, with the return through the body. Take the nominal 12 V for the current. The permitted voltage drop on this feed is 0.3 V. Copper resistivity is 0.0172 Ω·mm²/m. (a) Find the load current. (b) Find the minimum cross-section and choose a standard size. (c) Find the actual voltage drop with the chosen wire.
steps: Load current: the lamps are in parallel, so P = 2 × 55 W = 110 W and I = P ÷ V = 110 W ÷ 12 V = 9.17 A.
Only the feed carries resistance, because the body is the return, so l = 4.0 m.
Round up to the next standard size: 2.5 mm². (1.5 mm² is smaller than 2.10 mm², so it would break the voltage-drop limit.)
Resistance of the chosen wire: R = ρl ÷ A = 0.0172 × 4.0 ÷ 2.5 = 0.0275 Ω.
Actual drop: ΔU = I × R = 9.17 A × 0.0275 Ω = 0.25 V, which is below the permitted 0.3 V.
examples.answer: The current is 9.17 A; the minimum section is 2.10 mm², so a 2.5 mm² wire is chosen, giving a drop of 0.25 V (1.5 mm² would give 9.17 × 0.0172 × 4.0 ÷ 1.5 = 0.42 V, too much).

examples.question: On a rainy night in slow traffic a car's loads are: engine management and fuel pump 15 A, low beams 9.2 A, side and tail lamps 4 A, wipers 5 A, blower 12 A, rear-window heater 12 A, radio 2 A. At idle the alternator gives 45 A. (a) Find the battery discharge current. (b) Find the charge lost in 30 min. (c) On the highway the alternator gives 90 A with the same loads. If the battery needs 1.1 Ah of charge for each 1 Ah taken out, how long does the recharge take?
steps: Battery discharge current at idle = load − alternator = 59.2 A − 45 A = 14.2 A.
Charge lost in 30 min: Q = I × t = 14.2 A × 0.5 h = 7.1 Ah.
Charge to put back: 7.1 Ah × 1.1 = 7.8 Ah.
Spare alternator current on the highway: 90 A − 59.2 A = 30.8 A, all of which can flow into the battery.
Recharge time: t = 7.8 Ah ÷ 30.8 A = 0.25 h ≈ 15 min.
examples.answer: The battery discharges at 14.2 A and loses 7.1 Ah in half an hour; on the highway the 30.8 A surplus puts back the 7.8 Ah in about 15 minutes, so the trip keeps a positive charge balance only if the highway part lasts that long.

traps: Using the wire's route length when a separate return wire is used: the current goes out and back, so l is twice the route.
Rounding the cross-section down. Choose the next larger standard size, then check the actual drop.
A wire that passes the voltage-drop test can still overheat in a hot, packed harness; temperature is a separate test.
Terminal 30 is battery positive and terminal 31 is ground. Students who swap them read every circuit diagram upside down.

quiz.q: State the DIN 72552 meaning of terminals 15, 30, 31 and 50.
quiz.a: 15: ignition-switched positive; 30: battery positive, always live; 31: ground; 50: starter control.

quiz.q: Explain why the length in the wire-sizing formula doubles when a separate return wire is used.
quiz.a: The current flows through the feed and back through the return wire, so the resistive path is twice the route length. With chassis return only the feed counts.

quiz.q: A 120 W blower motor at 12 V is fed by a 2.5 m wire with body return. The permitted drop is 0.5 V and ρ = 0.0172 Ω·mm²/m. Find the minimum cross-section and pick a standard size.
A car stands for 21 days with a standby current of 30 mA. How much charge does it lose?
quiz.a: t = 21 × 24 = 504 h. Q = 0.030 A × 504 h = 15.1 Ah, a quarter of a 60 Ah battery.

quiz.q: A rear lamp is dim, but the bulb and fuse are good. Using a circuit diagram, explain where you would measure and what readings point to the fault.
quiz.a: Follow the path from terminal 30 or 15 through fuse, switch and connector to the lamp and on to ground 31. With the lamp on, measure the voltage drop across each section: more than a few tenths of a volt across a connector, switch or ground point locates the high resistance.

beyond: Not for the exam. Harnesses are among the heaviest electrical parts of a car, so makers now use aluminium for thick cables and zonal architectures in which a few zone controllers feed nearby loads through short wires; smart fuse boxes replace fuses and relays with semiconductor switches that report faults. Search for zonal E/E architecture and smart power distribution.
